notes: Wednesday 11 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Tue 10 Nov. Economy: US October CPI +0.4%, 10-year yield back near 5%, Waller flags possible 50bp December hike; Brent briefly under $90 on Iran-war-over hopes; SoftBank $7B quarterly loss; White House presses on tariffs after midterms. Tech (USA): Anthropic IPO $70–78, up to $1.4tn, trading Nov. 19; Nvidia hires Wachtell as shares slump and a shareholder lawsuit lands; CoreWeave beats and lifts guidance; Ring unveils indoor drone and Rover patrol robot. Politics: House 211–204 vote buries Hegseth impeachment; first day of Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi called constructive; Israel's new Knesset sworn in as Eisenkot tries to unseat Netanyahu; US boycotts UN human-rights review for a second year. Literature (USA): HOT Proulx, Maddow, Nelson books out; HOT Stylus Prize $750k to Graywolf, One Story, The Porch; NOT WeLib ordered to pay publishers $19.5m; NOT librarian and comics advocate Katharine Kan dies at 71. Social: Trinidad and Tobago anti-gay laws overturned; House report says US failures enabled Epstein after 2005; Board of Peace says Israel's Gaza flood-aid response is insufficient; FDA requires NAION vision warning on GLP-1 drugs.

stories.headline: US prices rose 0.4% in October, more than expected, and the 10-year Treasury yield raced back toward 5%
stories.dek: Core inflation also came in a bit hot. A Federal Reserve official said that if prices stay high, a bigger rate increase in December should be on the table.
stories.caveman: The US government said consumer prices rose 0.4% from September to October. Economists had expected 0.3%. That is slower than September's 0.6% jump, but still hotter than hoped. Core prices, which skip food and energy, rose 0.3%, also a bit above forecasts. After the report, the yield on the 10-year Treasury note — the rate that helps set mortgages and many loans — traded back above 5% before easing to about 4.99%. The 2-year yield, which tracks what people think the Federal Reserve will do next, jumped more than 0.18 percentage points. Fed Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London, said that if inflation keeps coming in high, officials should consider a 0.50 percentage-point rate increase in December, not just 0.25, or the Fed's credibility could be at risk. A weak auction of $42 billion in Treasury notes added to the selloff in bonds.
stories.why_it_matters: When the government has to pay more to borrow, mortgages, car loans and credit cards often get more expensive too. That is hard on households still angry about high prices after the midterm elections.
stories.camps: Some Fed officials want to hit inflation harder so it does not get stuck. Others worry that raising rates too fast could hurt jobs and the housing market. Markets now see a tighter path into 2027.
stories.image_alt: Traders watch US stock and bond moves on a busy market day

terms.explain: A monthly measure of how much a basket of everyday goods and services costs. If it rises, your money buys less.
The same price measure, but without food and energy, which jump around a lot. Officials watch it to see the underlying trend.
The interest rate the US government pays to borrow. When yields go up, bond prices fall, and many other loan rates often follow.
One hundredth of a percentage point. So 50 basis points is 0.50%.

stories.headline: Brent crude briefly slips below $90 for the first time since August after Trump says the Iran war is nearing an end
stories.dek: The global oil benchmark settled at $91.49, down about 1%. US crude settled at $86.04. Airline shares rose; oil companies fell.
stories.caveman: Oil prices dropped on Tuesday as markets took in President Donald Trump's comments that the nearly nine-month US war with Iran could end "fairly soon" and that Iran was "militarily … effectively over." Brent crude, the price used for most of the world's oil, briefly fell to $89.16 a barrel, the first time since August it had dipped under $90, and settled down 1.17% at $91.49. US West Texas Intermediate crude settled at $86.04. Oil had already fallen sharply on Monday. Trump also said Gulf countries would rather keep a naval blockade than see new fighting. Crude started this year near $60, then soared as high as $130 when strikes escalated in the spring. Airline stocks in Europe rose on hopes of cheaper fuel; BP and Shell shares fell. Markets have been extremely sensitive to any hint that the Iran conflict is easing or heating up again.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil feeds into gasoline, airfare and the cost of shipping goods. A lasting drop would ease some inflation pressure, but prices can snap back if peace talks fail.
stories.camps: Trump presents the war as basically over. Iran's leaders have been more cautious about whether talks are even happening. Energy traders are hopeful but not fully convinced.
stories.image_alt: Crude oil infrastructure as prices fall on hopes the Iran war is ending

terms.explain: The main international oil price, used as a benchmark for about 80% of the world's crude.
West Texas Intermediate, the main US oil price.
Using ships to stop another country from moving goods or weapons by sea.

stories.headline: SoftBank posts a $7 billion quarterly loss after a hit on US AI data-center equipment and a drop in Intel shares
stories.dek: The Japanese investment giant also booked a $3.7 billion loss over six months tied to changing plans for power gear at American projects.
stories.caveman: SoftBank, the big Japanese firm that pours money into technology companies, reported a net loss of 1.12 trillion yen, about $7 billion, for its fiscal second quarter. Part of the pain came from US artificial-intelligence data-center projects, and part from a fall in the value of its Intel shares. Over the six months ending September 30, it recorded a 597.2 billion yen, or $3.7 billion, loss after changing procurement plans for power-generation equipment meant for those US sites. SoftBank had bought equipment early because it feared shortages and long waits; by the end of September it had already paid $9.48 billion for power gear, including for a campus in Pike County, Ohio. Revenue still rose 13.3% over those six months, helped by telecom and AI computing. Its Vision Fund unit swung to a loss. SoftBank's stake in OpenAI was valued at $99.6 billion at the end of September, on $54.6 billion invested; a newer, higher OpenAI valuation had not yet been counted.
stories.why_it_matters: SoftBank is one of the biggest backers of the AI boom. A loss this large shows that building data centers is not just about chips — it is also about scarce electric power, and the bets can go wrong.
stories.camps: The company says it had to secure equipment early. Critics see another reminder that AI infrastructure is expensive, delayed and hard to finance. Investors will watch whether a higher OpenAI valuation later offsets the hit.
stories.image_alt: SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son at a public event

terms.explain: A Japanese company best known for investing in technology firms through its Vision Funds.
A building full of computers that run internet services and AI systems. They need huge amounts of electricity.
SoftBank's giant pools of money for investing in tech companies around the world.
The process of buying equipment or supplies, often far in advance.

stories.headline: The White House says it will keep Trump's tariffs going, even after voters punished Republicans over high prices
stories.dek: A former top Trump economic adviser called the tariffs "a consumption tax on the US consumer." A new poll found 62% of Americans want them repealed.
stories.caveman: One week after the midterm elections, in which high prices helped Democrats win, the White House said it would stay the course on tariffs — extra taxes on imported goods. Jim Goyer, who runs the White House Office of Public Liaison, told a business gathering in Washington that tariffs help rebuild US factories, protect supply chains and serve national security. "We are just getting started," he said. Later the same day, Gary Cohn, who was President Donald Trump's chief economic adviser in his first term, disagreed in public. "Tariffs are a consumption tax on the US consumer," he said, arguing that they raise prices and make people think twice about buying. A CNBC voter poll found about two-thirds of voters said Trump's policies added to inflation, and nearly nine in 10 said the cost of living was a major or crucial reason for their vote. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found 62% of Americans supported repealing the tariffs, and only 21% approved of Trump's handling of living costs.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs can protect some factories, but they often make imported food, clothes, parts and machines more expensive. That tension is now a central fight after the election.
stories.camps: The White House says the old trading system is gone and tariffs are here to stay. Many voters, and even some former Trump aides, say the policy is showing up in household bills.
stories.image_alt: Shipping containers at a US port, a symbol of tariff-affected trade

terms.explain: A tax on goods coming into a country. Importers usually pay it first, then often pass some or all of the cost on to shoppers.
A tax you pay when you buy something, rather than on your paycheck. Cohn is saying tariffs work like this for shoppers.
US elections in the middle of a president's term, when the whole House and part of the Senate can change hands.

stories.headline: Anthropic sets its IPO price at $70 to $78 a share and aims to start trading on November 19
stories.dek: At the top of the range the Claude-maker could be worth about $1.4 trillion and raise more than $64 billion, plus a $26 billion side deal with big tech firms including TSMC and Nvidia.
stories.caveman: Anthropic, the US company behind the Claude chatbot, filed a new price range for its stock-market debut: $70 to $78 a share for 825 million shares. People familiar with the plans said it aims to set the final price on November 18 and begin trading on November 19. At the high end it could raise up to $64.35 billion and be worth as much as $1.405 trillion, counting all shares and options — huge, but below the $2 trillion some backers had talked about earlier this year. Anthropic also arranged a $26 billion private sale of stock, at the same price as the IPO, to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. About 20% of the IPO is aimed at ordinary investors, more than the usual 5% to 10%. The timing is rocky: last week's midterm elections and worries about high interest rates have made investors more nervous about paying for giant AI buildouts.
stories.why_it_matters: This would be one of the biggest market debuts ever. If the stock soars, it could restart excitement about AI companies; if it stumbles, it would feed doubts that the spending boom can pay off.
stories.camps: Bulls point to huge demand and a long list of famous backers. Skeptics note that earlier $2 trillion talk has been walked down, and midterm politics could slow new data centers.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic's office or branding as the company prepares to go public

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a company sells shares to the public and lists them on a stock exchange.
What the whole company is said to be worth, based on the share price times all the shares.
A sale of shares to chosen investors, not through the public offering itself.
The slice of new shares reserved for ordinary individual investors, not just big funds.

stories.headline: Nvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate Jensen Huang's affair; shares fall again and investors sue
stories.dek: The board named former federal prosecutor Joon H. Kim to lead the probe. The stock dropped about 6% on Tuesday after a 4% fall on Monday.
stories.caveman: Nvidia's independent board members said they have hired the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and attorney Joon H. Kim, a former acting US attorney in Manhattan, to investigate CEO Jensen Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. Huang has admitted an affair with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed. US officials have been reported as concluding she was tied to Chinese intelligence. The FBI is also investigating. Nvidia shares fell about 6% on Tuesday, after more than 4% on Monday, as investors worried the investigation could force the co-founder and CEO out. A shareholder lawsuit filed in federal court in San Jose, California, accuses Nvidia and Huang of misleading investors about the relationship and about Megaspeed, which has faced questions over whether Nvidia chips were diverted to China. Nvidia has said it studied Megaspeed's chip deployments. The company has been under pressure from critics and lawmakers over what it knew.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia makes the chips that power most leading AI systems. If its CEO were forced out, or if export rules tightened further, the shock would move through the whole tech economy, including Taiwan's supply chain.
stories.camps: The board says it wants a thorough, independent investigation. Huang's supporters argue he should stay and that customer meetings are normal. Investors and some politicians want clearer answers about China and succession.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose board has hired a law firm to investigate

terms.explain: A review run by outside lawyers, not by the CEO's own team, meant to look at what happened without taking his side.
A case in which investors accuse a company or its leaders of hiding important facts and hurting the stock.
A Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. It has been accused, and Nvidia has disputed, of helping send chips to China.

stories.headline: AI cloud company CoreWeave beats revenue forecasts and raises its outlook, easing some slowdown fears
stories.dek: Revenue jumped 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier. The company still lost $709 million and is carrying almost $47 billion in debt.
stories.caveman: CoreWeave, a US company that rents out Nvidia chips in the cloud so other firms can run AI, reported stronger third-quarter results than Wall Street expected and raised its forecast for 2026. Revenue soared 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier. The company still posted a net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 a share, wider than the $110 million loss a year ago. It now expects 2026 revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion and adjusted operating income of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion, both higher than its August guidance and higher than analysts' estimates. The stock rose after hours. Even so, CoreWeave has lost more than 40% of its market value in the past month. Some of its bonds recently yielded more than 16%, a sign lenders are nervous. The company ended the quarter with almost $47 billion in debt. Its finance chief said it does not plan to issue more parent-level unsecured debt through 2027 at today's yields, and will lean on customer prepayments and loans tied to specific assets.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a test of whether the companies building AI data centers can keep growing even as borrowing gets more expensive. Strong demand is encouraging; the debt pile is the worry.
stories.camps: Bulls say the numbers show AI demand is still real. Skeptics note the company is losing money and owes a huge amount, so a tight credit market could still squeeze it.
stories.image_alt: CoreWeave leadership at a public forum as the company reports earnings

terms.explain: A US "neocloud" company: it buys expensive AI chips and rents the computing time to other businesses.
A company's own forecast of future sales or profits, which investors use to judge whether business is speeding up or slowing down.
Borrowed money that is not tied to a specific building or machine as collateral. It is usually riskier, so lenders demand higher interest.

stories.headline: Amazon's Ring unveils a $250 indoor flying camera and a $1,000 robot to patrol offices and warehouses
stories.dek: The textbook-sized drone follows a preset path when an alarm goes off, then flies itself back to its charger. It is not allowed to go outside.
stories.caveman: Ring, the Amazon-owned doorbell-camera company, introduced two new security gadgets on Tuesday. The Ring Drone Cam costs $250. It is a small indoor drone that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, when a window, door or other sensor is triggered, or when the owner sends it. It can fly for up to eight minutes, then return to its charging dock by itself. CEO Jamie Siminoff said the built-in lights could scare off someone outside at night. The drone is noisy, and Ring says it cannot legally fly outdoors under US aviation rules. The company also launched the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, a wheeled security robot based on Amazon's older Astro home robot, meant to patrol offices, warehouses and other workplaces. It has a rising camera, a siren, two-way audio and a light that shines on the ceiling so people can see where it is. Ring, which Amazon bought in 2018, has faced years of privacy criticism, including over police partnerships. It says an LED light flashes when the devices are recording.
stories.why_it_matters: A camera that flies around your house, or rolls around a workplace, collects far more than a doorbell video. The tools may deter crime, but they also deepen questions about who is being watched, and who else can see the footage.
stories.camps: Ring says one moving device can replace many fixed cameras, and that privacy is the default. Civil-liberties critics have long argued Ring is too close to police and too eager to put cameras in private spaces.
stories.image_alt: Ring's indoor security drone hovering in a hallway

terms.explain: A company Amazon bought in 2018, best known for video doorbells and home security cameras.
Amazon's earlier home robot, now being reused as the base for Ring's workplace patrol robot.

stories.headline: The House votes 211–204 to send Pete Hegseth's impeachment to committee, effectively killing the effort
stories.dek: Republican Thomas Massie forced the vote a day after filing eight articles. Almost no time remains before Democrats take over Congress in January.
stories.caveman: The US House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to send impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to a committee. That move almost certainly means the House will not vote on actually impeaching him before this Congress ends. The effort was started Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who often breaks with President Donald Trump. Massie accused Hegseth of waging war without Congress's approval, of extrajudicial killings in Caribbean boat strikes against suspected drug smugglers, and of going after Sen. Mark Kelly, a military veteran, in a way that chilled free speech. House Republican leaders wanted the effort stopped. CNBC reported that every Republican except Massie voted to send it to committee, and that all Democrats voted against that referral, because they wanted the impeachment to keep moving. Trump then claimed the effort had "miserably FAILED" and called it an "EXONERATION." Democrats take control of the House and Senate in early January, leaving little time for this Congress to act.
stories.why_it_matters: Impeachment is how Congress can try to remove a Cabinet official. Burying the vote means there will be no full House judgment on Hegseth's conduct in the Iran war and other operations before power changes hands.
stories.camps: Trump and Republican leaders call the case a stunt. Massie and Democrats say the charges deserved a real debate, not a procedural burial. Hegseth's office said he followed lawful presidential orders.
stories.image_alt: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose impeachment bid was blocked in the House

terms.explain: A formal charge by the House that a president or other official committed serious wrongdoing. The Senate would then hold a trial.
A procedural vote that sends a measure off the floor and into a committee, which can let it die quietly when time is short.
Done outside the courts. Critics use this word when they say killings happened without a legal trial or clear authority.

stories.headline: Zelensky calls the first day of Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi "constructive"; a second day follows
stories.dek: US officials said Moscow and Kyiv were showing a little flexibility on who would control Ukraine's east after a war. Prisoner exchanges were also discussed.
stories.caveman: Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States met for about four hours in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first of two days of talks aimed at ending Russia's full-scale war. President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not in the room, said the discussion had been "constructive and quite substantive." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking from Paris, called it "very productive." Officials on the scene were tight-lipped. US officials had said earlier that both sides were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on who would control Ukraine's eastern regions after a war. Zelensky said humanitarian issues, including prisoner-of-war exchanges, were discussed. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates the US had "narrowed the gaps" and hoped to move toward a solution that ends the war. Kushner and Steve Witkoff are part of the US team. Expectations for a sudden breakthrough remain low. Talks were due to continue on Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: A real opening in talks could mean fewer deaths and a path to rebuilding. A weak deal, though, could lock in territorial losses and leave Ukraine less secure.
stories.camps: The US presents itself as a broker narrowing differences. Ukraine wants security guarantees, not just a ceasefire. Russia has not publicly shown that it will give up its core demands.
stories.image_alt: Officials gather for Ukraine-Russia-US talks in Abu Dhabi

terms.explain: Meetings with three sides at the table. Here that means Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
A soldier captured by the other side in a war. Exchanges send some of those people home.
Areas in eastern Ukraine, including places Russia occupies or claims, that are a core dispute in any peace deal.

stories.headline: Israel's new parliament is sworn in as Gadi Eisenkot tries to assemble a government and oust Netanyahu
stories.dek: Eisenkot's bloc won 48 seats, Netanyahu's 53 — both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot has 28 days, plus a possible two-week extension.
stories.caveman: Israel's newly elected parliament, the Knesset, was sworn in as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief, tries to form a government and replace caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Eisenkot received more formal recommendations from lawmakers than Netanyahu, so he has been given the first chance, even though not all of his backers want to govern together. In October's election, Eisenkot's four-party bloc won 48 seats and Netanyahu's bloc won 53, so neither has the 61 needed for a majority. Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension. Almost half of the new members did not serve in the last parliament, and Arab-led parties have a record number of seats. After the swearing-in, Netanyahu warned against a government that depends on Arab parties, and called for a national-unity government to face what he called the threat of a nuclear Iran. Eisenkot called that speech "delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful" and said Netanyahu was unfit to stay in office. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a coalition is formed, which could take weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever forms the next government will shape the war's aftermath, Gaza policy, and talks with Israel's neighbors. A long stalemate would leave a caretaker in charge at a volatile moment.
stories.camps: Netanyahu's camp says only a unity government, without Arab parties, is safe. Eisenkot's camp says voters wanted a change and that Netanyahu should go. Smaller parties will hold the bargaining power.
stories.image_alt: Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with trying to form a government

terms.explain: Israel's parliament. It has 120 seats. A government usually needs at least 61 supporters.
The person who keeps running the government after an election, until a new coalition is agreed.
An alliance of parties that together have enough seats to govern, because no single bloc won a majority.

stories.headline: The United States boycotts its UN human-rights review for a second year, the first country ever to skip twice
stories.dek: Washington has already left the Human Rights Council, but the review is supposed to be mandatory for every UN member. The ACLU and other groups still showed up in Geneva.
stories.caveman: The United States left an empty chair at the United Nations' universal periodic review in Geneva, a process in which every country's human-rights record is examined by other countries every few years. It is the second year in a row the US has skipped, and the first time any UN member has failed to appear twice. Israel once skipped a review in 2013 and came back nine months later; no country had missed two. Civil-society groups still traveled to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU's Jamil Dakwar said the Trump administration was violating rights "unabashed," pointing to the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and LGBTQ people, and warned that the administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." The State Department replied that the US has withdrawn from the 47-member Human Rights Council, which it accuses of "anti-American rhetoric." Leaving the council, though, does not cancel the review, which is supposed to cover all 193 UN members. The UN has few ways to punish a no-show. Rights groups want the review to go ahead anyway, using evidence already submitted.
stories.why_it_matters: If the most powerful country can skip a review that is meant to apply to everyone, the idea that no government is above scrutiny gets weaker — and other governments may copy the tactic.
stories.camps: The US administration says the council is biased and hostile. Rights groups say that is a reason to show up and argue, not to walk away, and they see a wider pattern of leaving international bodies.
stories.image_alt: The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva, where the US left an empty chair
stories.image_credit: Photo: Lian Yi / Xinhua via Getty Images

terms.explain: A UN process in which every member country's human-rights record is examined, in turn, by other countries.
A 47-country UN body that meets in Geneva on human-rights issues. The US has formally withdrawn from it.
The American Civil Liberties Union, a US group that goes to court and to international forums to defend civil rights.

stories.headline: HOT: A big Tuesday for US books — Annie Proulx's stories, Rachel Maddow on the Justice Department, Willie Nelson on late-life art
stories.dek: Literary Hub's list of 20 new titles also includes novels by Chinelo Okparanta and Gabriel Bump, and a study of journalist Janet Malcolm.
stories.caveman: Tuesday was a packed release day in US publishing. Annie Proulx, the author of The Shipping News and the story that became the film Brokeback Mountain, published New and Selected Stories from Scribner, mixing classic work with three new stories. MSNBC host Rachel Maddow released Department of Fate, a history of the US Justice Department. Willie Nelson published The Last Leaf, about making art later in life. Other notable arrivals include Chinelo Okparanta's novel This Impossible Life, Gabriel Bump's Don't Stop Snowing, James Gleick's history of the telephone, and Eve Sneider's The Absent Woman, about the late journalist Janet Malcolm. (Dustin Hoffman's memoir also came out; it was already getting reviews this week.) For readers trying to catch up before the holidays, it is a mixed table: serious nonfiction, a career-spanning story collection, and new fiction.
stories.why_it_matters: Publication day is when books actually reach stores and libraries. A cluster of well-known names can set the conversation for the rest of the year, especially as awards season continues.
stories.camps: Some readers are here for Proulx's fiction. Others want Maddow's account of American law and power, or Nelson's reflections. The risk of a celebrity-heavy season is that quieter novels get less space.
stories.image_alt: Covers and new titles featured in Literary Hub's list of books out November 10

terms.explain: A book that gathers an author's best older short stories and adds some new ones, often as a career landmark.
The US government department that runs federal prosecutors and much of the country's top law enforcement. Maddow's book is about its history.

stories.headline: HOT: A new Stylus Prize gives $250,000 each to Graywolf Press, One Story magazine, and Nashville's Porch Writers' Collective
stories.dek: The Literary Arts Fund asked writers across the US to nominate the nonprofits that actually help them work. The awards are unrestricted cash.
stories.caveman: The Literary Arts Fund, marking one year since it launched, announced the first winners of its Stylus Prize, a new award for literary nonprofits. The three honorees are Graywolf Press, a respected Minnesota publisher; One Story, a magazine devoted to short stories; and The Porch Writers' Collective, a community group in Nashville. Each will receive $250,000 to spend as they choose, for a total of $750,000. Nominations were gathered anonymously from writers around the country. Money for the prize comes from philanthropic groups led by the Mellon Foundation, which last year pledged $50 million to nonprofit literary arts through 2030. Fund director Jen Benka said these groups run workshops, festivals, magazines and books, and help writers meet readers. One Story's founders called the award "a transformational moment" and said it would help them plan beyond immediate bills. The news lands in a period of tight budgets and disappearing public arts funding.
stories.why_it_matters: Most literary groups live on small grants and donations. An unrestricted quarter-million dollars can keep a magazine or press going, raise pay, or fund the next few years of programs.
stories.camps: Writers and small publishers are celebrating. Some in the wider arts world will watch whether a few headline winners are enough, given how many other local groups are also struggling.
stories.image_alt: Announcement of the inaugural Stylus Prize for literary nonprofits

terms.explain: A grant the recipient can spend as it sees fit, not tied to one narrow project.
A well-known nonprofit literary publisher based in Minnesota.
A US literary magazine that publishes short stories and also mentors writers.

stories.headline: NOT: A US court orders pirate site WeLib to pay 13 publishers $19.5 million and tells its hosts to take it down
stories.dek: The default judgment, entered November 9 in Manhattan, mirrors a similar $19.5 million ruling against Anna's Archive earlier this year. Publishers say WeLib copied that site.
stories.caveman: A federal judge in New York has ordered the pirate book site WeLib to pay 13 publishers $19.5 million. Judge Victor Marrero also told the companies that register and host its web addresses to take the site offline, after the operators never answered the lawsuit. In a default judgment entered November 9, the court awarded the maximum damages for willful copyright infringement: $150,000 for each of 130 works. Each publisher listed 10 titles, so each is owed $1.5 million. In May, another judge in the same court issued the same kind of $19.5 million default judgment against Anna's Archive, a similar site whose operators also never showed up. Publishers say WeLib copied Anna's Archive's code and much of its collection, and tried to make money by offering AI companies high-speed access to pirated books and papers. The Association of American Publishers helped organize the June suit, filed by houses including Penguin Random House, HarperCollins, Hachette, Macmillan, Simon & Schuster, and education and science publishers such as Elsevier, Pearson and Wiley. WeLib claimed to hold more than 43 million books and 98 million papers.
stories.why_it_matters: Free piracy sites undercut authors and publishers, and they are also becoming a source of text for AI training. Winning a judgment is one thing; actually collecting the money and keeping a site offline is harder.
stories.camps: Publishers call the sites businesses, not libraries, especially when faster downloads cost money. Open-access advocates argue that lawsuits do not fix high book and journal prices, and that shadow libraries often reappear under new names.
stories.image_alt: Publishers Weekly report on a court order against the pirate site WeLib

terms.explain: A court ruling entered because the other side never showed up to defend itself.
An amount of money set by copyright law, not by proving exact lost sales. The maximum here was $150,000 per work.
Another large pirate library for books and papers. Publishers already won a similar judgment against it this year.

stories.headline: NOT: Katharine Kan, the librarian who spent decades getting comics onto US library shelves, has died at 71
stories.dek: She died on October 12 after working until weeks before her death. In the 1980s she had to argue just to buy trade-paperback comics for teenagers.
stories.caveman: Katharine "Kat" Kan, a librarian who helped make comics a normal part of American libraries, has died at 71. Publishers Weekly reported the news on November 10; she died on October 12. Her husband wrote that she refused to retire until her health forced her to, only weeks before her death. Kan was born in Tokyo in 1955 and trained as a librarian in Hawaii. She led young-adult services in the Hawaii State Library system, later worked in Indiana and in Panama City, Florida, and advised library suppliers on graphic novels. She also wrote a long-running comics column for a library journal. In a 2011 interview she recalled that in the mid-1980s her system would not buy comic books, even as staff wondered how to get teenage boys back into libraries. She pushed to buy trade paperbacks like Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and Elfquest, then watched boys discover that a librarian their mom's age loved comics too. "It all started from there," she said, "and I ended up becoming an 'expert' by default."
stories.why_it_matters: Many adults now treat graphic novels as serious reading, but that shift in libraries was fought for by people like Kan, one shelf at a time.
stories.camps: Colleagues remember her as persistent and generous. Her career also shows how slowly institutions change: what is obvious now was once against the rules.
stories.image_alt: Katharine Kan, librarian and advocate for comics in libraries

terms.explain: A book-length comic, often sold in libraries and bookstores rather than as a floppy pamphlet.
A standard bookstore-format paperback. In the 1980s, some libraries would buy comics in this form even when they would not buy periodical comic books.

stories.headline: A UK court overturns Trinidad and Tobago's laws against same-sex intimacy after an 11-year fight
stories.dek: The Privy Council, the islands' final court of appeal, said the colonial-era rules violated the right to private and family life. Campaigner Jason Jones brought the case.
stories.caveman: London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which still acts as Trinidad and Tobago's highest court of appeal, has struck down laws that made consensual same-sex intimacy a crime. The judges said the laws did not respect "the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life." The case was brought by Jason Jones, 62, a dual citizen, who has been fighting for 11 years. He won in Trinidad's High Court in 2018, but the government appealed and that ruling was overturned. This is the first time the Privy Council has decided a case that decriminalizes same-sex intimacy. Campaigners hope it will help similar challenges in other Commonwealth countries. About 34 Commonwealth nations still have colonial-era laws against homosexuality; some include prison, and in some places the death penalty. Trinidad's attorney general had argued that old British laws were locked in by "savings" clauses at independence. The judges unanimously sided with Jones. Lord Sales said the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual."
stories.why_it_matters: A court victory does not instantly change everyday life, but it means the state can no longer treat private same-sex relationships as a crime. It may also encourage cases in other countries that still use these old laws.
stories.camps: Jones and other campaigners call it a step toward full equality. Opponents had tried to keep the old criminal rules in place. The ruling is about the criminal law, not yet about marriage or every other legal right.
stories.image_alt: Campaigner Jason Jones, who spent 11 years challenging Trinidad and Tobago's anti-gay laws

terms.explain: A London court that still serves as the final court of appeal for some countries that were once British colonies, including Trinidad and Tobago.
aliases: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

terms.explain: To stop treating something as a crime. Here, consensual same-sex intimacy is no longer a criminal offense.
Legal language that kept old British colonial laws in force after a country became independent, making them harder to challenge.

stories.headline: A House report says US federal authorities could have stopped Jeffrey Epstein's crimes after 2005, but failed
stories.dek: The Republican-led Oversight Committee blames poor judgment, Epstein's influence, and a 2007 deal that let him avoid a federal prosecution.
stories.caveman: The US House Oversight Committee, led by Republicans, released a final report on Tuesday about how investigators and prosecutors handled Jeffrey Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell. It concludes that crimes Epstein committed after 2005 could have been prevented if federal authorities had not failed. The report is based on 15 months of interviews, government files and financial records. Epstein died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex-trafficking charges. The committee said some failures were poor judgment by the US Attorney's Office, and others seemed to flow from Epstein's wide influence. Instead of fully investigating allegations in other states, the US Attorney's Office in Southern Florida made a 2007 agreement that allowed Epstein to avoid a federal prosecution. On his death, the report pointed to staffing shortages, poor record-keeping and lax security at the jail, and said testimony could not fully settle every question, including a gap in surveillance video. The Justice Department, the report said, also failed at communicating about the release of documents.
stories.why_it_matters: Survivors have said for years that powerful people were protected and that later abuse was allowed to continue. An official finding that the crimes were preventable puts that failure on the record.
stories.camps: The committee presents this as a long, bipartisan-relevant failure of the justice system. Others will argue over which officials deserve the most blame, and whether the report goes far enough on Epstein's network.
stories.image_alt: Jeffrey Epstein, whose case a House committee says was mishandled for years
stories.image_credit: Photo: Corbis via Getty Images / BBC

terms.explain: A powerful committee in the US House of Representatives that investigates how government agencies do their jobs.
Recruiting, moving or holding people for sexual exploitation. Epstein was awaiting trial on these charges when he died.
The federal prosecutor's office in a region. The one in Southern Florida made the 2007 deal with Epstein.

stories.headline: Trump's Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods is still "insufficient"
stories.dek: Heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents. The UN says about 1.4 million people in Gaza, around 65% of the population, now live in tents or makeshift shelters.
stories.caveman: The Board of Peace, a US-backed body set up to oversee President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan, called on Israel to immediately let all needed humanitarian supplies into Gaza after heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents. In a rare public criticism of Israel, the board said it recognized steps Israel is considering, but "the response remains insufficient." It said delays in approving shelter, water and sanitation supplies made a foreseeable winter emergency worse, and also delayed work to disarm Hamas and transfer authority. Israel's military agency that coordinates aid said it had let in tens of thousands of tents and trucks of winter supplies, but that reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms." On Sunday, three children and a woman were killed when a sand bank collapsed onto tents in the central Strip. The UN says about 65% of Gaza's people, around 1.4 million, now live in tents or makeshift shelters after being displaced by Israel's military campaign. Residents described sewage overflowing into flooded tents and said they had no dry bedding or food.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter rain on damaged ground turns already unsafe tents deadly. If aid stays slow, more people can die from exposure and disease even when active fighting is not the day's headline.
stories.camps: The Board of Peace says Israel must open the crossings now. Israel says aid is going in and that rebuilding depends on Hamas disarming. People living in the tents say they have already waited too long.
stories.image_alt: Flooded tents and stormy weather making life harder for displaced families in Gaza

terms.explain: A US-backed body created to oversee Trump's Gaza peace plan, including aid and a political transition.
Things people need to survive in a crisis, such as tents, food, water, medicine and sanitation equipment.
Forced to leave home because of war or disaster, often into tents or crowded shelters.

stories.headline: The FDA tells makers of Wegovy, Zepbound and other GLP-1 drugs to warn about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden vision loss
stories.dek: The agency found a possible higher risk of NAION, but says a direct cause has not been proven. Eye doctors say do not stop the medicine without talking to a physician.
stories.caveman: The US Food and Drug Administration is requiring new safety warnings on all GLP-1 drugs — the popular medicines used for diabetes and weight loss, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound. The concern is a rare condition called NAION, which happens when blood flow to the front of the optic nerve drops and can cause sudden, sometimes permanent, vision loss, often in one eye. The FDA said cases have been reported with every GLP-1 drug now on the market, but a cause-and-effect link has not been established. In a review of 126 trials involving more than 134,000 patients, there were 6.4 NAION cases per 100,000 patient-years among GLP-1 users, compared with 3.8 among people on other treatments or a placebo. Diabetes itself also raises NAION risk, which makes the numbers harder to read. Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, said it still does not believe a causal link is proven. Eli Lilly, which makes Mounjaro and Zepbound, said it is reviewing the update. The American Academy of Ophthalmology said any added risk appears small and patients should not stop the drugs on their own, but should see an eye doctor quickly if they notice sudden, painless vision loss.
stories.why_it_matters: Tens of millions of people use these drugs. A rare side effect can still affect many people at that scale, so a clear warning helps patients notice symptoms early without causing a panic.
stories.camps: Regulators want the risk on the label. Drugmakers say the benefit still outweighs a rare, unproven harm. Eye doctors urge caution and quick treatment of symptoms, not a sudden rush to quit.
stories.image_alt: GLP-1 injection pens of the kind now required to carry a new vision-loss warning

terms.explain: A class of drugs that copy a gut hormone. They help control blood sugar and appetite. Brand names include Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound.
Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy: a rare problem in which the optic nerve does not get enough blood, causing sudden vision loss that can be permanent.
The US Food and Drug Administration, the agency that decides what warnings must appear on medicine labels.
